title: Supreme Court: Balance Sheet Entries Acknowledging a Debt Restart the Limitation Clock
meta_description: Supreme Court revives a recovery suit, holding balance sheet entries that carry forward a debt create a fresh limitation period under Section 18.
bench: Vikram Nath, Augustine George Masih and Sandeep Mehta, JJ.
case_name: Yusuf v. Vigyapan Loke Delhi Advertising Co-operative Group Housing Society Ltd.
citation: 2026 INSC 1207, arising from SLP(C) No. 30778/2024 (Delhi High Court, CRP 66/2020, order dated 4 November 2024)
body: On 6 November 2026, a three-judge bench of the Supreme Court comprising Justices Vikram Nath, Augustine George Masih and Sandeep Mehta set aside a Delhi High Court order that had stood in the way of a recovery suit filed by one Yusuf against Vigyapan Loke Delhi Advertising Co-operative Group Housing Society Ltd. The judgment, reported as 2026 INSC 1207, arose from an appeal against the High Court's order of 4 November 2024 in CRP 66/2020.

Yusuf had sued the Society to recover money he said it owed him. The Society resisted on the ground that the claim was barred by limitation, the usual three-year window under the Limitation Act, 1963 having long since closed. What kept the claim alive, Yusuf argued, was that the Society's own balance sheets, filed in later years, continued to carry forward the very liability he was suing to recover, which in law amounts to the Society acknowledging that it still owed the money.

The High Court had not accepted this and ruled against Yusuf, closing off the suit. The Supreme Court disagreed. It held that an entry in a balance sheet which carries forward an outstanding liability operates as a written acknowledgment of a subsisting debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and that such an acknowledgment, made before the earlier limitation period expires, starts the clock running again from that date. The bench held this acknowledgment need not name the creditor for it to count; it is enough that the entry shows the liability still exists.

The Court also rejected the argument that reviving a time-barred claim this way requires a separate application to condone the delay. Section 18 operates automatically: once a qualifying acknowledgment is on record, a fresh limitation period follows from the date of that acknowledgment, without any further step by the creditor. The bench cautioned, though, that a balance sheet cannot be read in isolation. Its entries must be examined together with the accompanying notes, qualifications and the auditor's report, since those can confirm or contradict what a bare figure in a ledger seems to show.

On that basis, the Court held that Yusuf's suit could not have been shut out at the threshold. Whether the balance sheet entries the Society filed genuinely acknowledged the specific debt Yusuf claims, and how much of it remains payable, are questions for the trial court to work out on evidence, not something decided by rejecting the plaint. The suit stands revived and goes back for trial, with every issue on the merits left open.

The ruling builds on a line of cases the Court has developed over several years, among them Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd v. Bishal Jaiswal in 2021 and a 2025 ruling in an IL&FS matter, both holding that balance sheet entries can amount to acknowledgment of debt even without naming the creditor. Yusuf's case confirms that this reasoning applies just as much to an ordinary civil recovery suit between private parties as it does to claims pursued through insolvency proceedings, where the same principle has already been used to keep financial creditors' claims alive against defaulting borrowers.

The judgment is also a reminder of how narrow the threshold inquiry under Order VII Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure is meant to be. A court examining whether a plaint discloses a cause of action must confine itself to the plaint and the documents filed with it, and cannot weigh disputed questions of fact, such as whether a particular balance sheet entry truly refers to this creditor's debt, as if it were conducting the trial itself. Those questions belong to evidence and cross-examination, not to a preliminary objection meant only to weed out suits that disclose no claim at all.

The practical lesson cuts both ways. Anyone owed money in India, including an NRI who lent funds before moving abroad or a family business chasing an old due from a cooperative society or a counterparty, gains a real argument to keep a stale claim alive wherever the debtor's own accounts keep showing the liability. Debtors, equally, have reason to look closely at how their accountants carry forward old entries, since an unexamined line in a balance sheet can hand a creditor years of extra time to sue. A society, company or individual that genuinely disputes owing anything would do well to say so clearly in its accounts, rather than let a routine entry sit unexplained for years.
why_it_matters: Creditors chasing old dues in India, including NRIs collecting on loans made before they moved abroad and family businesses pursuing long-pending claims, now have Supreme Court authority that a debtor's own balance sheet can keep a claim alive well past the usual three-year limitation period, even if the creditor is never named in the entry. Debtors, including companies and cooperative societies, should treat old liabilities carried forward in their accounts as live legal exposure rather than a bookkeeping formality, since an unexplained entry can reopen a claim many believed had lapsed.
card_summary: Supreme Court revives a recovery suit, ruling that a debtor's balance sheet entries carrying forward a liability count as acknowledgment of debt, resetting the limitation period even without naming the creditor.
card_tip: Assuming an old debt has lapsed once the usual three-year limitation period passes. Check whether the debtor's own balance sheets kept carrying forward that liability in later years.
verification_notes: AUDIENCE: NRI / domestic creditor recovering money lent. TARGET QUERY: can I still recover an old debt in India if the limitation period has passed. DEMAND EVIDENCE: none seen (no search-volume or trending data was available; topic chosen for its freshness and practical relevance to anyone recovering dues in India after a long gap). Bench, date, citation and core holding (balance sheet entries as acknowledgment of debt under Section 18, creditor need not be named, no condonation application required) confirmed across Verdictum, LiveLaw, Courtbook and ThePrint. The underlying dispute (Yusuf's recovery suit against the Society, the limitation defence, the High Court's order of 4 November 2024 in CRP 66/2020 against him) confirmed via ThePrint's report, corroborated by the Supreme Court's own case listing describing the appeal as arising from CRP 66/2020. Left out: the amount Yusuf claims is due and the precise nature of the underlying transaction, since sources described the parties inconsistently (as a builder in one place and a contractor in another) and no source confirmed a figure from two independent reports; these are left for the trial court in any event.
